body: Greek licence plates are either all white or have the standard European design. Taxis have yellow licence plates.
The Greek language features a unique alphabet. It shares similarities with both the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, but lowercase letters often have softer shapes.
Greek utility poles are primarily wooden, often with a distinct dark brown color. They are also often noticeably taller than in other countries.
Distinctive poletops with a metal frame shaped vaguely like a harp are unique to Greece.
Many poles in Greece have five vertical insulators.
Small lamps with a round shade above the bulb are found on poles in Greece. This type of lamp is also found in North Macedonia and Serbia.
Slightly faded, solid white double middle lines are common in Greece. This helps distinguish it from other Mediterranean countries.
Yellow road lines are more common in Greece than in any other southern European country.
Greek bollards are wedge-shaped with almost square reflectors, which are red on the front and white on the back.
Greek chevrons have white arrows on a black background. Similar designs are found in Albania, Italy, and the UK.
Greek warning signs have a red border and a yellow background.
Greek directional signs are typically blue and arrow-shaped. Place names are written in Greek with a yellow font and in English with a white font.
Greek town entry signs are white with thick horizontal blue stripes at the top and bottom.
Greek kilometre markers are blue, with "km" written in both the Latin and Greek alphabets.
Greek pedestrian signs feature two dotted horizontal lines instead of the usual vertical stripes.
Miniature churches on small pedestals are often found along roadsides and are unique to Greece.

Greek architecture is typically Mediterranean, with white and pastel-coloured houses and orange tiled roofs. A recognizable style, especially on islands, features white houses with blue fences, window frames, and doors. Urban buildings are often multi-storied with connected balconies.
Greece is very mountainous, with much of the coverage on winding mountain roads.
Red dirt is very common in Greece, but is also found in Albania.
Greece has Generation 4 "smallcam" coverage, which is lower and has a large, sometimes transparent, circular blur with a small protrusion.
Greece has a lot of Generation 3 winter and fall coverage, which often has a bleak look.
Greece has many islands, but coverage is not guaranteed on all of them. While mainland Greece and Crete have all camera generations, most other islands do not.
Greek area codes start with a 2. The third digit often indicates the largest city (1) or its surrounding area (9).
The largest flat agricultural valleys are near Thessaloniki and Larissa. Smaller flat valleys are found elsewhere in the north and center.
The tallest mountains and most high-altitude mountain roads are in the western half of Greece.
The iconic Greek architecture of completely white walls with blue doors and shutters is mainly found on the central Cyclades islands.
Many central islands, especially the smaller ones with coverage, have a very barren landscape with small bushes and no trees.
Olive plantations are common in coastal areas, especially on Crete and the southern Peloponnese.
Citrus plantations are mainly found in coastal areas, particularly on the southern Peloponnese.
A unique car antenna with a slight bulge at the tip can be found on Crete.
Mount Pangaion is a recognizable solitary mountain located south of a flat agricultural valley.
The extraordinary monolithic mountains of Meteora are found north of Trikala.
Yellow taxis are found in Athens.
Blue taxis with a white roof are found in Thessaloniki.
In Thessaloniki, you will often see a large number of unusually tall antennas on top of buildings.
